newsitem.title: BURUNDI: African sanctions team arrives in Burundi.
newsitem.headline: African sanctions team arrives in Burundi.

text.p: A delegation from regional countries that have imposed sanctions on Burundi arrived in the capital Bujumbura on Friday to review efforts by military ruler Major Pierre Buyoya to meet their demands.
It was the first time a delegation had visited since regional African presidents imposed sanctions six days after a bloodless coup that brought Buyoya to power on July 25.
Diplomats and aid workers said the visit by East African ministers could break a deadlock over the conditions for regional states to lift the economic and transport embargo.

The delegation was led by Tanzania's foreign minister Jakaya Kikwete and was to meet Buyoya, Burundi's ethnic Hutu prime minister, and national assembly officials, according to U.N. Special Envoy for Burundi Marc Faguy.
"We have a message to deliver to the Burundian authorities. That message is for them and we will deliver it to them only," Kikwete told reporters at the airport in Bujumbura.
Zaire's deputy prime minister, Kititwa Tumansi, said the visit would not amount to recognition of Buyoya's government.
"We recognise the state of Burundi as a republic but that does not mean we recognise its regime," Tumansi told reporters.

The delegation included Kenya's ambassador to Tanzania, Uganda's foreign minister, a Tanzanian diplomat who is head of the sanctions committee, Cameroon's ambassador to Ethiopia and a representative of Tanzanian mediator Julius Nyerere.

The regional ministers cancelled a planned visit on Wednesday in response to an announcement by Burundi's regime that it would not start unconditional talks with Hutu rebels until the blockade was lifted.

The cancellation reflected a growing rift between Buyoya's isolated government and regional heads of state demanding a return to constitutional legality in Burundi where ethnic war has killed 150,000 people in three years.

Regional states imposed the embargo on landlocked Burundi on July 31 in response to a coup by the army that ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Hutu, and installed Buyoya of the minority Tutsi tribe, which dominates the military.
Earlier this month the states decided to maintain the blockade, setting a one month deadline for the start of unconditional all-party negotiations.
On Thursday, Burundi's Brarudi brewery, a chief source of government revenue, said it had suspended distribution and could stop its operations because of a lack of fuel and spare parts.
Revenue from Brarudi pays civil service salaries.

At a summit last Saturday regional leaders rejected a suggestion by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to ease the embargo. Instead they gave Burundi one month to enter negotiations with Hutu rebels or face further sanctions.
They also decided to send a ministerial committee to Burundi to review a stated commitment by Buyoya to unconditional talks.
